title: DateTime timezone not found in database
author: Stefan Bogdanescu
excerpt: # DateTime timezone not found in database The error `DateTime::__construct(): Failed to parse time string ... The timezone could not be found in the database`...
content:
# DateTime timezone not found in database

The error `DateTime::__construct(): Failed to parse time string ... The timezone could not be found in the database` is a classic PHP trap that often stems from how the operating system handles timezone data rather than a flaw in your application logic. You are likely concatenating user inputâspecifically a date, time, and a timezone offset like `America/New_York`âinto a single string before passing it to the `DateTime` constructor. While this approach seems intuitive, it relies entirely on PHP's internal list of recognized timezones being up to date with your server's configuration.

When you pass a string containing an IANA timezone identifier (like `America/New_York`) directly to the `DateTime` constructor without first setting the default timezone or ensuring the system has the latest database of timezone definitions, PHP attempts to parse that specific offset against its local list. If the underlying `tzdata` package on your server is outdated, or if the server's default timezone setting conflicts with the one you are trying to use, the parser fails immediately at the position of the timezone string. This results in a fatal exception that halts execution, preventing any further processing of the datetime object.

The root cause here is usually missing or stale timezone data on the host machine. PHP uses the `datetime` package from the IANA Time Zone database to resolve these identifiers. If your server runs an older version of this data, it won't recognize newer timezone rules or specific region codes that have been updated in recent years. The fix isn't to change the application code to avoid using timezones; it is to ensure the environment supports them correctly.

To resolve this, you must update the timezone database on your server. On Linux distributions like Ubuntu or Debian, this often involves updating the `tzdata` package:

```bash
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install --reinstall tzdata
# Or for CentOS/RHEL
sudo yum reinstall tzdata
```

Once the package is updated, you may need to restart your web server or PHP-FPM service to ensure the new definitions are loaded. However, there is a more robust architectural decision to make when building applications that deal with dates and times: avoid relying on string concatenation for timezone parsing whenever possible.

Instead of constructing a single string like `"01/18/2016 00:00 AM America/New_York"`, it is best practice to handle the date components separately or ensure your input sources provide data in ISO 8601 format (e.g., `2016-01-18T00:00:00-05:00`). If you must work with legacy forms that submit separate fields for time and timezone, explicitly set the default timezone in your PHP environment before instantiating the object. You can do this using `date_default_timezone_set()`:

```php
date_default_timezone_set('UTC'); // Or any valid IANA zone
$datetime = new DateTime($inputString);
```

This ensures that if the parser encounters ambiguity or relies on a fallback, it does so within a known context. Furthermore, consider moving away from parsing strings entirely and instead validating the timezone input against a whitelist of allowed zones before processing. This prevents invalid inputs from reaching the constructor and adds a layer of defense against unexpected timezone data in your database.

If you are using Laravel, the framework provides helper methods that abstract much of this complexity. Utilizing Carbon or Laravel's built-in `now` helpers with explicit timezone arguments can significantly reduce the risk of parsing errors compared to raw `DateTime` instantiation. For instance, setting the application timezone in `config/app.php` ensures a consistent baseline across your entire stack.

Ultimately, the "timezone not found" error is an environmental issue masquerading as a code problem. Updating your system's timezone data and adopting stricter input validation strategies will eliminate these exceptions and make your datetime handling resilient to future updates in IANA rules.
